transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi… thanks for seeing me. I guess the main thing is my sleep. It’s probably not the worst problem, but it’s gotten pretty unreliable. Even when I go to bed exhausted, I end up lying there going over sales forecasts or team issues in my head, and then I’ll wake up around 3 or 4 and I just… can’t get my brain to shut off again. I wasn’t sure if that was enough of a reason to come in, but it’s starting to wear on me.
When you’re lying awake, do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I try to tell myself it’s just being responsible, but most days my mind kind of jumps around. Like, whether we’re going to hit the launch numbers, then whether someone on my team is unhappy and might quit, then the mortgage, or a client renewal… and it’s like any small delay starts feeling like it could turn into something much bigger. I don’t know if that counts as “a lot,” but it feels like a lot in my head.
Do you find yourself worrying like this about many different parts of your life, not just work?

Yeah… it’s not only work, I guess. Work is the easiest thing to point to, but my mind kind of jumps around from launch numbers to whether someone on my team is upset or might leave, and then suddenly I’m thinking about the mortgage or whether a client renewal could fall through. It’s like any little delay or uncertainty starts to feel like it could become a much bigger problem. I’m probably making it sound dramatic, but that’s what it feels like.
When you start worrying, do you find it hard to stop or control the worry?

Yeah… I do, more than I’d like to admit. I can tell myself, like, “Brenda, you’ve made the plan, you’ve done what you can, just let it go,” and that works for maybe five minutes. Then I’m back in some other loop. It’s like I check one concern off and three more pop up. I know that probably sounds a little silly, but it’s hard to make it stop.
How long have you been worrying like this most days?

Um… I guess it’s been most days for a while. It started building after the sales division reorganization, so… about thirteen months ago now. I kept thinking it would settle down once things stabilized, but it’s kind of stayed with me. Does that answer what you mean?
Do you feel these symptoms started because of the sales division reorganization?

I think so, yes. I mean, I don’t want to overstate it like everything is because of that, but that’s when I really noticed it starting to build. Since the sales division reorganization… so about thirteen months ago, it’s just been more of a most-days kind of thing. Does that make sense?
Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling down or depressed?

I… don’t think so? Not depressed, exactly. I mean, I’ve had some rough days and I get worn out, but I wouldn’t say I’ve been feeling down most of the time over the last couple weeks. Is that what you mean?
Have you been feeling restless or keyed up?

Yeah… I think so. I try not to make a big deal of it, but I do feel pretty wound up a lot of the time. Like, even if I’m just at home eating dinner, it feels like I’m still sitting in a pipeline review or waiting for something to go wrong. My shoulders are tight almost constantly, even when I’m trying to relax. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
If the work reorganization had never happened, do you think you would still be worrying this much?

I’m not totally sure, but… probably not this much. I think I’ve always been someone who thinks ahead, maybe overprepares a little, but it really started building after the sales division reorganization — about thirteen months ago. That’s when it became more noticeable to me, anyway. Does that answer it?
Do you feel your level of worry is more than most people would have in response to the work reorganization?

Probably… yes. I don’t love saying that, because the reorg was stressful for everyone, and I know that. But my mind seems to run with it more than it should. Most days it jumps from, like, whether we’ll hit the launch numbers, to whether someone on my team is about to quit, then somehow to the mortgage or a client renewal. And even a small delay starts feeling like it could turn into something major. I’m not sure if that’s more than “normal,” but it feels like maybe it is.
Did your worrying begin within three months after the sales division reorganization?

Yes… I think it did. Not immediately the next day or anything, but within a few months after the reorganization, the worrying started building. And it’s been kind of going on since then — about thirteen months now, I guess. Does that sound like what you’re asking?
Are these worries causing problems in your day-to-day functioning?

Yeah… I think it is, though I don’t want to overstate it. At work, I spend so much time second-guessing decisions that things like pipeline reviews can get tense, or I slow things down because I’m trying to make sure I’m not missing something.

And then at home, by the time I get there, I’m just… drained. I’m more reactive than I want to be, and I don’t feel as present with my husband. So yes, it’s affecting things. Is that the kind of problem you mean?
Aside from the work reorganization, do you find yourself worrying excessively about other parts of your life?

Yes… I mean, I think it started with the reorganization, but it doesn’t stay neatly in that box. Most days my mind kind of jumps around — from whether we’ll hit the launch numbers, to whether someone on my team might quit, then suddenly I’m thinking about the mortgage or a client renewal.

I know some of that is reasonable to think about, but it feels like I latch onto it too hard. Like even a small delay can start feeling like it’s going to turn into something much bigger. Is that what you mean by other parts of life?
If work felt stable again, do you think you would still be worrying this much?

I’d like to say no, honestly… that if work settled down, I’d settle down too. But I’m not totally sure that’s true.

Even when one thing is okay, my mind kind of finds the next thing — like whether we’ll hit the launch numbers, or if someone on my team is thinking of quitting, and then it’ll jump to the mortgage or a client renewal. It’s like small delays don’t just feel small; they start feeling like they could turn into something major.

I know that probably sounds a little dramatic, but that’s kind of how it feels.
If the work reorganization were completely resolved, do you think you’d still be worrying this much?

I think… probably yes, at least to some extent. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, but my worry doesn’t really stay in one lane.

Even if the reorganization were fixed, most days my mind would still jump from, like, whether we’ll hit the launch numbers, to whether someone on my team is about to quit, then to the mortgage or a client renewal. And then a small delay starts feeling like it could turn into something major.

So… yes, I think I’d still be worrying. Maybe not exactly the same amount, but more than I’d like. Does that answer it?
When you can’t sleep, is your mind usually filled with worry?

Yes… usually, yes. I try not to make it into a bigger thing than it is, but that’s honestly a big reason I came in.

Even when I go to bed exhausted, my mind starts replaying forecasts, team issues, things I said or need to handle. And then I’ll wake up around 3 or 4 and it’s like my brain turns back on immediately, and I can’t really power it down again.

I don’t know if that’s the kind of thing you mean, but it’s been pretty unreliable.
On nights when you can’t sleep, do you ever find that you’re not worrying about anything in particular?

Not usually, no. I mean, I guess there are moments where it feels more like just… being awake and frustrated that I’m awake. But most of the time, if I’m lying there or waking up at 3 or 4, my mind is on something.

It’s usually work things — forecasts, team issues, things I need to fix or might have missed. Even if I went to bed exhausted, it’s like my brain starts running again and I can’t get it to power down.

I don’t know if I’m explaining that right, but it’s not often just blank insomnia.
